questions.question: Which Shakespeare play mentions the Great Bed of Ware?

questions.explain: The bed, over 3 metres wide, is mentioned in 'Twelfth Night'. Visitors carved their initials into it.

questions.question: Stolen from Vienna in 2003, how was Cellini's gold Saliera found in 2006?
questions.hint: It was hidden outdoors, not in any building.
questions.explain: Cellini's gold salt cellar, stolen from the Kunsthistorisches Museum in 2003, was found buried in a wooden case in 2006.

questions.question: What happened to the Portland Vase, an ancient Roman glass vessel, in 1845?
answers: It survived a shipwreck at sea
It cracked in a house fire
It was flown across the Atlantic
A visitor smashed it to pieces
questions.hint: It has had to be restored three times since.
questions.explain: In 1845 a drunken visitor smashed it at the British Museum. It has been restored three times since.

questions.question: The Areni-1 shoe, the oldest known leather shoe, was found stuffed with what?
questions.hint: It may have kept the shoe's shape, like an early shoe tree.
questions.explain: Grass, which may have kept its shape. The shoe, about 5,500 years old, is a European size 37.

questions.question: Norway's 1999 stamp for Johan Vaaler's paperclip patent shows which clip design?
questions.hint: Surprisingly, the clip shown was never Vaaler's own design.
questions.explain: The stamp shows the Gem clip, never Vaaler's design. His own 1899 clip was clumsier and never produced.

questions.question: Where has the Centennial Light, a hand-blown bulb, glowed almost continuously since 1901?
questions.hint: It is in the United States.
questions.explain: In a Livermore fire station. It turned 125 in 2026, having burned for more than a million hours.

questions.question: The word 'zipper' was coined in 1923 to sell which product?
questions.hint: It was something you wore.
questions.explain: The B.F. Goodrich company coined 'zipper' in 1923 for rubber galoshes that closed with a slide fastener.

questions.question: The teddy bear is named after which US president?
questions.hint: He refused to shoot a bear tied to a tree on a 1902 hunt.
questions.explain: Theodore Roosevelt refused to shoot a bear tied to a tree in 1902. A Brooklyn shopkeeper then sold 'Teddy's bear'.

questions.question: What gave George de Mestral the idea for Velcro?
questions.hint: Tiny hooks were the secret he copied.
questions.explain: Burrs. Their tiny hooks clung to clothing; de Mestral copied the trick and patented hook-and-loop tape in 1955.

questions.question: What problem was the Post-it Note first meant to solve?
answers: Bookmarks slipping out of a hymnal
questions.hint: The trouble involved a book.
questions.explain: Art Fry's bookmarks kept slipping out of his hymnal, so he used Spencer Silver's weak 1968 adhesive.

questions.question: Why did the Coca-Cola formula sit in a New York bank vault, 1919–25?
questions.hint: The reason was financial.
questions.explain: It was collateral for a loan. Since 2011, the company says, it has been in its Atlanta museum's vault.

questions.question: In 1901, two Milwaukee women filed a patent for an early form of what?
questions.hint: Their invention was a mesh pocket for a single cup.
questions.explain: Roberta Lawson and Mary McLaren filed their 'tea-leaf holder' patent in 1901, before Thomas Sullivan's 1908 silk samples.

questions.question: Melitta Bentz made her first coffee filter from paper taken from what?
questions.hint: It was blotting paper, used to soak up ink.
questions.explain: Blotting paper from her son's exercise book. The firm she founded in 1908 still bears her name.

questions.question: In 2010, 168 bottles of what were raised from a Baltic shipwreck?
questions.hint: It was made in France.
questions.explain: Champagne, including Veuve Clicquot and Juglar. After more than 150 years on the seabed, experts could still taste it.

questions.question: What could scientists read from a 5,700-year-old lump of chewed Danish birch pitch?
questions.hint: Chewing leaves more behind than toothmarks.
questions.explain: It held enough DNA to read its chewer’s complete genome. Birch pitch was a prehistoric glue; chewing may have softened it.

questions.question: What keeps the air out of the Speyer bottle of Roman wine?
questions.hint: Think of something that floats.
questions.explain: A layer of oil. Sealed about 1,700 years ago, the bottle was found in a Roman grave at Speyer in 1867.

questions.question: What is written on YBC 4644, a Babylonian clay tablet at Yale?
answers: A map of the night sky
questions.hint: Think of food.
questions.explain: Recipes for stews and broths, set down by about 1730 BC: with its sister tablets, the oldest known recipes.

questions.question: How were Chicken Ramen, the first instant noodles, made 'instant'?
questions.hint: It was quick and hot, not cold or slow.
questions.explain: Flash-fried: in 1958 Momofuku Ando fried seasoned noodles in hot oil, in a shed behind his home in Ikeda.

questions.question: What did Harvard Law School pay in 1946 for what proved an original Magna Carta?
questions.hint: They thought it was only a copy, so it came cheap.
questions.explain: Just $27.50. In 2025 it proved one of only seven known originals of Edward I's 1300 reissue.

questions.question: Which of these continents is missing from the Behaim Globe, made in the early 1490s?
questions.hint: It shows the world as Europeans knew it before Columbus.
questions.explain: The oldest surviving globe, made in Nuremberg in the early 1490s, has no America. Its nickname, Erdapfel, means 'earth apple'.

questions.question: The Bayeux Tapestry is misnamed. What is it really?
questions.hint: Its base cloth is linen.
questions.explain: It is a hand-stitched embroidery on linen, nearly 70 metres long, not a woven tapestry.

questions.question: According to carved graffiti, what did P. Abbott do in the Coronation Chair in 1800?
questions.hint: The graffiti's date spans two days: 5–6 July.
questions.explain: It reads 'P. Abbott slept in this chair 5-6 July 1800'. Westminster schoolboys and tourists carved names too.

questions.question: What was the Antikythera mechanism, recovered from a shipwreck?
answers: A bronze lock from a temple
questions.hint: It is more than 2,000 years old.
questions.explain: A Greek bronze gear machine over 2,000 years old. It predicted eclipses and even tracked the Olympic Games.

questions.question: The Lycurgus Cup looks opaque green. What colour does it glow when light shines through?
questions.hint: Tiny traces of gold and silver in the glass cause it.
questions.explain: Red. Tiny amounts of gold and silver make the 4th-century Roman cup opaque green, but red when lit through.

questions.question: Looted in 1999, the Nebra sky disc was recovered in 2002 by whom?
questions.hint: The recovery took place in Switzerland.
questions.explain: Basel police recovered it in 2002. About 3,600 years old, it is the oldest known concrete depiction of the sky.

questions.question: Joseph Lister dropped his carbolic spray. Which germs did he decide mattered more than airborne ones?
questions.hint: Think of what actually touches a wound.
questions.explain: Lister later abandoned the spray: germs on dressings and whatever else touched the wound mattered more than airborne ones.

questions.question: In 1938, which car maker began giving British hospitals iron lungs built at his works?
questions.hint: He was a British car maker.
questions.explain: Lord Nuffield's Morris Motors works built the iron lungs, to a largely plywood design by Edward Both of Adelaide.

questions.question: How long could bulky clinical thermometers take to give a reading before Allbutt's 1860s design?
questions.hint: Long enough to be a nuisance for a busy doctor.
questions.explain: Up to 20 minutes. Clifford Allbutt's 15 cm thermometer took about five minutes and was easy to carry.

questions.question: Which disease, declared eradicated in 1980, was defeated partly with a forked needle?
questions.hint: Its vaccine story began with cowpox.
questions.explain: Smallpox. The forked needle held a small drop of vaccine between its prongs; its great virtue was simplicity.

questions.question: Why does the Broad Street pump replica in Soho have no handle?
answers: Handles were melted down in wartime
Its builders ran out of money
questions.hint: It recalls events in Soho in September 1854.
questions.explain: In 1854 John Snow traced cholera to the pump and persuaded officials to remove its handle. The replica has none.

questions.question: In 1816, why did René Laennec begin listening to patients' chests through a tube?
answers: A new law banned touching patients
Pressing his ear there felt awkward
questions.hint: His own account mentions a young woman patient.
questions.explain: Finding it awkward to press his ear to a young woman patient's chest, Laennec listened through a tube: an early stethoscope.

questions.question: Why did Norman Heatley design stackable ceramic vessels for Oxford's penicillin team?
answers: The team ran short of bedpans
questions.hint: Before these, they had used a container from hospital wards.
questions.explain: Oxford's team grew penicillin mould in bedpans; when they ran short, Heatley designed stackable ceramic vessels.

questions.question: What is the handle of Napoleon's toothbrush made of?
questions.hint: It is a precious metal with a golden finish.
questions.explain: Silver gilt, engraved with a crowned N. It came to the Science Museum Group from Henry Wellcome's collection.

questions.question: Why was the Penny Black, the first adhesive postage stamp, replaced within a year?
answers: Its black ink faded in sunlight
Its red cancellation could be removed
It was too big for envelopes
questions.hint: The problem showed up after the letters were posted.
questions.explain: Its red cancellation could be removed and cleaned stamps reused; black ink barely showed on black. Enter the Penny Red.

questions.question: What did Stuart Weitzman add to the back of the British Guiana One-Cent Magenta?
answers: A smiley face and a date
questions.hint: Its owners have marked its back; his mark reflected his trade.
questions.explain: Shoe designer Stuart Weitzman drew a stiletto and added his initials while he owned the stamp, 2014–21.

questions.question: How many 1933 gold Double Eagle coins may legally be privately owned?
questions.hint: Auction reports call it a unique coin.
questions.explain: Just one. It sold at Sotheby's in 2021, setting a world record for a coin at auction.

questions.question: What did William Robey pay in 1918 for a sheet of 100 Inverted Jenny stamps?
questions.hint: He paid face value, like any post office customer.
questions.explain: $24, in May 1918, for 100 new airmail stamps with the biplane upside down. One fetched $2 million in 2023.

questions.question: In 1868 the United States paid for Alaska with a single cheque. Which country received it?
questions.hint: Look west across the Bering Strait.
questions.explain: Russia. The Treasury warrant for $7.2 million was dated 1 August 1868. Critics called it 'Seward's Folly'.

questions.question: What was being burned when the Houses of Parliament caught fire in 1834?
questions.hint: The fuel came from a centuries-old way of keeping the nation's accounts.
questions.explain: Two cartloads of Exchequer tally sticks, wooden receipts for government income, were burned in stoves under the House of Lords.

questions.question: How did ownership of a big rai stone, the stone money of Yap, usually pass?
questions.hint: Big ones seldom moved, even when they changed hands.
questions.explain: Big rai stones seldom moved: ownership passed by common agreement. Yapese crews quarried them on Palau, some 400 km away.

questions.question: From 1644 Sweden struck copper plate money. Roughly what did a 10-daler plate weigh?
questions.hint: It was cash, but hardly something to carry in a pocket.
questions.explain: A 10-daler plate weighed almost 20 kilos; such unwieldy cash helped prompt Europe's first banknotes, in 1661.

questions.question: Onto what was the 1860 recording of 'Au clair de la lune' scratched?
questions.hint: Think of a surface darkened by a smoky flame.
questions.explain: Scratched into soot-blackened paper in 1860; played back too fast in 2008, it sounded like a girl.

questions.question: A Halberstadt organ began one John Cage piece in 2001. When is it due to end?
questions.hint: The opening silence alone lasted 17 months.
questions.explain: The performance began in 2001 and is due to end in 2640; weights, not fingers, hold the notes down.

questions.question: The 'Lady Blunt' Stradivari violin was sold in 2011 to raise money for what?
answers: Sending a violin to the Moon
questions.hint: The cause was far from Europe.
questions.explain: It was sold in 2011 for Japan's earthquake and tsunami relief, fetching over four times the previous Stradivari auction record.

questions.question: Why does the Stroh violin have a metal horn instead of the usual wooden body?
answers: To survive salt water at sea
To play well in extreme cold
So it could be played underwater
To be loud enough for recording
questions.hint: Its horn points the sound in one direction, towards a new machine.
questions.explain: A Stroh violin: a diaphragm and metal horn take the place of the usual wooden body, making it loud enough for early gramophone recording.

questions.question: According to a 2002 Oxford DNA study, which bird is the dodo's closest living relative?
questions.hint: The dodo belonged to the same family as a common city bird.
questions.explain: The Nicobar pigeon, according to a 2002 Oxford DNA study. The Oxford Dodo's head skin and foot scales are the only dodo soft tissue known to survive.

questions.question: SUE the T. rex wears a cast skull. Roughly what does the real one weigh?
questions.hint: It weighs more than three grown men put together.
questions.explain: The real skull, about 270 kg, sits in its own case so visiting scientists can study it more easily.

questions.question: In 1992, what did the Peekskill meteorite hit in New York State?
questions.hint: Its target had wheels but was going nowhere.
questions.explain: It hit a parked car; more than a dozen videos caught its fireball, letting scientists reconstruct its orbit.

questions.question: The Natural History Museum's blue whale stranded in Ireland in 1891. What did the museum pay?
questions.hint: A Victorian clerk would find it steep; a national museum, affordable.
questions.explain: It stranded near Wexford in 1891; the museum bought it for £250, then stored it for over four decades.

questions.question: Who called the 1911 Antarctic trek for emperor penguin eggs 'the worst journey in the world'?
questions.hint: He was one of the three men on the trek.
questions.explain: Apsley Cherry-Garrard, one of the three men on the trek, called it that; three emperor penguin eggs made it back.

questions.question: In 1954, after crashing through an Alabama roof, whom did the Hodges meteorite bruise?
questions.hint: It bounced off a household radio on the way down.
questions.explain: It crashed through the roof, bounced off a radio and bruised a napping woman; it later served as a doorstop.

questions.question: Marie Curie's 1899–1902 laboratory notebook is still contaminated with which substance?
questions.hint: It has a half-life of about 1,600 years, so it will linger.
questions.explain: Radium-226 still contaminates the notebook, now kept in London's Wellcome Collection.

questions.question: How were two of Darwin's notebooks returned to Cambridge University Library in 2022?
answers: By courier, with a ransom note
Through a New York auction house
Dug up in a college garden
questions.hint: They came back anonymously, with a seasonal greeting for the Librarian.
questions.explain: Missing for over 20 years, they came back in 2022 in a pink gift bag, with a 'Happy Easter' note.

questions.question: How many drops of Brisbane's pitch drop experiment has anyone ever watched fall?
questions.hint: Even a custodian who kept watch for decades never saw one.
questions.explain: It has run since 1927, yet nobody has watched a drop fall; custodian John Mainstone kept watch for 52 years.

questions.question: The Oxford Electric Bell, labelled 'Set up in 1840', still rings. What powers it?
questions.hint: Nobody dares open the power source to see what is inside.
questions.explain: It still rings on its original batteries; nobody knows exactly what they contain, and opening them might end it.

questions.question: Whose chalk has covered a lecture blackboard, kept unwiped in Oxford since May 1931?
questions.hint: The sums on it concern the size of the expanding universe.
questions.explain: Einstein's chalk sums estimate the density and size of the expanding universe; the board has stayed unwiped since May 1931.

questions.question: Which city's museum keeps Galileo's cracked telescope lens, pieced together from fragments?
questions.hint: The museum there is named after Galileo himself.
questions.explain: Museo Galileo in Florence keeps it; the museum says it is the lens through which he found Jupiter's moons.

questions.question: Why was a marble metre set into a Paris wall in the 1790s?
answers: To teach citizens the new unit
To record the Seine's flood levels
To mark the city's old boundary
As a finishing line for races
questions.hint: It was one of 16 put up around Paris where passers-by would see them.
questions.explain: It was put up so citizens could learn the new unit, and it is still at 36 rue de Vaugirard.

questions.question: In which year did the Royal Society receive the Newton reflecting telescope it owns today?
questions.hint: It arrived decades after Newton's death.
questions.explain: The telescope Newton made in 1671 left the Royal Society's care; the one it owns now arrived in 1766.

questions.question: What is Le Grand K, which defined the kilogram until 2019?
questions.hint: It is made of metals, not stone, and none of them is gold.
questions.explain: Le Grand K is one platinum-iridium cylinder, kept near Paris under three glass bell jars in a three-key vault.

questions.question: Which mission carried tree seeds around the Moon in 1971, later grown into 'Moon Trees'?
questions.hint: The same mission's commander famously played golf on the Moon.
questions.explain: Apollo 14's seeds burst from their container in a vacuum chamber back on Earth, but grew anyway.

questions.question: Ireland's Apollo 11 Moon rock survived a trip from the Moon but not what?
answers: A crash on its delivery flight
A burglary at the US embassy
A drop onto a stone floor
A fire at a Dublin observatory
questions.hint: The building it was kept in was badly damaged in 1977.
questions.explain: It survived the trip from the Moon, but not the 1977 fire at Dublin's Dunsink Observatory.

questions.question: What is the Rijksmuseum's so-called 'Moon rock', a 1969 gift, really?
questions.hint: Tests in 2009 showed it never left Earth.
questions.explain: Petrified wood. The US ambassador gave it to ex-prime minister Willem Drees in 1969; tests in 2009 exposed it.

questions.question: What do the etched diagrams on the Voyager Golden Record's cover explain?
questions.hint: Think of what a finder would need before hearing Earth's sounds.
questions.explain: Both Voyager probes carry a gold-plated copper record of Earth's sounds and images; the cover explains how to play it.

questions.question: Who paid to develop the Fisher space pen, adopted by NASA in 1967?
questions.hint: NASA was a customer, not the one who paid for development.
questions.explain: Paul Fisher's company paid, reportedly about $1 million; NASA adopted the pen in 1967 and the Soviets bought 100.

questions.question: In 1966, who found the stolen World Cup trophy wrapped in newspaper in London?
questions.hint: The finder's name is also something you might keep in a jar.
questions.explain: A dog called Pickles found it wrapped in newspaper in south London in March 1966.

questions.question: In 1895 the original FA Cup was stolen from a Birmingham shop. Who held it?
questions.hint: The holders played in the same city as the shop.
questions.explain: Aston Villa held it; the trophy, which had cost £20 to make, was never recovered despite a £10 reward.

questions.question: At the first modern Olympics, Athens 1896, what medal did winners receive?
questions.hint: There was no gold at those Games.
questions.explain: Winners at Athens 1896 received a silver medal and an olive branch; third place got no medal at all.

questions.question: Which trophy's engraving misspelled Boston's 1972 champions as the 'Bqstqn Bruins'?
questions.hint: The Bruins are an ice hockey team.
questions.explain: The Stanley Cup's engravings include typos; Jacques Plante won it five years running and was spelled differently each time.

questions.question: The 1930 World Cup final reportedly used each team's ball for one half. Who won?
questions.hint: The hosts won, after trailing at half-time.
questions.explain: Argentina led 2-1 at half-time; after the ball swap, Uruguay won 4-2.

questions.question: The Ashes urn lives at Lord's. What does the winning team receive?
answers: The original urn for a year
questions.hint: Think of what a team could take home while the original stays put.
questions.explain: The winners receive a replica; the urn itself, given to England captain Ivo Bligh in 1882-83, stays at Lord's.

questions.question: The Calcutta Cup, England and Scotland's rugby trophy, was made from what?
answers: Silver rupees from a disbanded club
questions.hint: The metal came from a club in Calcutta that had closed down.
questions.explain: It was made from 270 silver rupees left by a disbanded Calcutta club, with cobra handles and an elephant lid.

questions.question: A Babylonian tablet from 177 BC sets out rules for which ancient board game?
questions.hint: By 177 BC the game was already over 2,000 years old.
questions.explain: The tablet gives rules for the Royal Game of Ur; the British Museum calls them the oldest known board-game rules.

questions.question: Which word did the 1631 'Wicked Bible' leave out of the seventh commandment?
questions.hint: Without it, a ban turns into an instruction.
questions.explain: Missing 'not', the seventh commandment read 'Thou shalt commit adultery'; printer Robert Barker was hauled before a court and fined.

questions.question: Why did Cambridge researchers train the world's first webcam on the Trojan Room coffee pot?
answers: To see if it was empty
questions.hint: Think of what the researchers were tired of finding.
questions.explain: In 1991 Cambridge researchers rigged the camera to spare themselves wasted trips to an empty pot.

questions.question: What warning did the label on Tim Berners-Lee's NeXT computer, the first web server, give?
answers: Do not play games on it
questions.hint: Think about what a server must keep doing, day and night.
questions.explain: It ran the world's first website; the label was there to stop anyone switching it off.

questions.question: How much was the only known Nintendo PlayStation prototype bought for, at a bankruptcy auction?
questions.hint: Think of a bargain-bin price, not a collector's price.
questions.explain: It was bought for $75 and sold in 2020 for $360,000, including the buyer's premium.

questions.question: Which keyboard layout did the Sholes & Glidden typewriter of 1874 introduce?
questions.hint: Most English-language keyboards still use it today.
questions.explain: It introduced QWERTY. Made by the gunmakers Remington, it typed only capitals.

questions.question: Why was the Apple-1 computer priced in repeating sixes?
questions.hint: Nothing sinister: think of the co-founder's taste in numbers.
questions.explain: Steve Wozniak liked repeating digits, and had no thought of the Devil. Some 200 were made, sold without a case; the Smithsonian has one.

questions.question: Roughly how many vacuum tubes did ENIAC, the 30-ton computer of 1946, use?
questions.hint: The machine filled a large room, but not a whole building.
questions.explain: The original used some 18,000 vacuum tubes; decades later, Penn students recreated it on a single chip.

questions.question: What did the 'hotline' button on Sony's first Walkman, the 1979 TPS-L2, switch on?
questions.hint: Sony expected listeners to share their music with a friend.
questions.explain: It switched on a microphone for chatting; a second headphone socket let a friend plug in.

questions.question: What was the shell of the first computer mouse, built for Douglas Engelbart, made of?
questions.hint: A natural material, the kind carpenters work with.
questions.explain: Wood. SRI engineer Bill English built it for Douglas Engelbart.

questions.question: Hanafuda, Japanese 'flower cards', were the first product of which company, founded in Kyoto in 1889?
questions.hint: The company turned to video games only in the 1970s.
questions.explain: Nintendo began making hanafuda in Kyoto in 1889, and turned to video games only in the 1970s.

questions.question: When Britain's Harwell atomic centre no longer needed its Dekatron computer, how did it pick a new owner?
questions.hint: Its next home was a college in Wolverhampton.
questions.explain: A competition: the college with the best plan for it won. A Wolverhampton college renamed it WITCH.

questions.question: Where was the answer to the final code on the CIA's Kryptos sculpture found in 2025?
questions.hint: Think of who knew the answer from the very start.
questions.explain: It lay among the artist's own papers, held in a Smithsonian archive: found, not cracked.

questions.question: What exposed Yale's Vinland Map, a supposed 15th-century chart of America, as a fake?
questions.hint: Yale's scientists looked closely at what the lines were drawn with.
questions.explain: Its ink contains titanium, which dates it to the 1920s or later; Yale confirmed the forgery in 2021 after analysing the whole map.

questions.question: The Louvre's 'ancient' Tiara of Saitaphernes was in fact recent work. Its goldsmith came from the area of which city?
questions.hint: The goldsmith worked near lands where Scythians once lived.
questions.explain: A goldsmith from the Odessa area had made it recently. Unmasked in 1903, it is still in the Louvre's collection.

questions.question: The Maya Codex of Mexico, long dismissed as a fake, is a calendar tracking which planet?
questions.hint: It follows a planet often seen shining at dawn or dusk.
questions.explain: It is a Venus calendar, and probably the oldest surviving manuscript from the Americas.

questions.question: In 2004, who was called in to crack the letters OUOSVAVV on Shugborough's Shepherd's Monument?
questions.hint: Think of wartime experience rather than academic or puzzle expertise.
questions.explain: Bletchley Park veterans, who had worked on Enigma codes in the war, thought it a classical reference. They did not expect a quick answer.

questions.question: The Smithsonian's Wizard of Oz ruby slippers are a mismatched pair. Who recovered their stolen twins?
questions.hint: An American law enforcement agency, part of the US Justice Department.
questions.explain: The two shoes come from different sets. Their missing twins, stolen in 2005, were recovered by the FBI in 2018.

questions.question: In 1958, how did Harry Winston send the Hope Diamond to the Smithsonian in Washington?
questions.hint: The method was surprisingly ordinary: the same service anyone could use.
questions.explain: By registered mail, in a small brown-paper parcel, delivered in Washington by a letter carrier.

questions.question: From 1913 until 1977, where did the Tarkhan Dress, the oldest known woven garment, lie unrecognised?
answers: In a pile of dirty linen
questions.hint: It was overlooked among other old textiles, not hidden away.
questions.explain: It lay in a pile of dirty linen. Radiocarbon dates its linen to 3482–3102 BC; signs of wear suggest it was worn.

questions.question: The Black Prince's Ruby, on the Imperial State Crown, is really which gemstone?
questions.hint: A red gem long confused with ruby; its name is less well known.
questions.explain: It is a red spinel, not a ruby, set in the Imperial State Crown.

questions.question: How far into its maiden voyage in 1628 did the Swedish warship Vasa sink?
questions.hint: Think of a short walk, not a day's sailing.
questions.explain: About 1,300 metres. Thirty men had run across its deck; it rolled so badly they stopped, but it sailed anyway.

questions.question: How deep did the wreck of Shackleton's Endurance lie when it was found in 2022?
questions.hint: Deeper than Ben Nevis is high, more than twice over.
questions.explain: It lay 3,008 metres down in the Weddell Sea. Sea ice crushed it in 1915; its name was still legible.

questions.question: What speed did the steam locomotive Mallard reach in its record run of 1938?
questions.hint: Faster than two miles a minute, but not three.
questions.explain: 126 mph on 3 July 1938, still the world steam speed record. Mallard had been built in Doncaster that year.

questions.question: Which school keeps the James Caird, the lifeboat Shackleton sailed to South Georgia in 1916?
questions.hint: It was Shackleton's own old school, in London.
questions.explain: Dulwich College, his old school. After Shackleton died in 1922, a school friend, John Quiller Rowett, gave it to the college.

questions.question: Which language calls a bicycle a 'rower', after the maker of the 1885 Rover safety bicycle?
questions.hint: The 'w' in 'rower' is pronounced like an English 'v'.
questions.explain: Polish. The word comes from Rover, whose safety bicycle, made in Coventry in 1885, set the modern shape.

questions.question: Boeing built the three Apollo lunar rovers, now official historic landmarks, in which US city?
questions.hint: It is in Washington State.
questions.explain: Kent, Washington. Boeing built the rovers there for Apollo 15, 16 and 17, and all three are still on the Moon.

questions.question: How many climbers died when the Matterhorn's first-ascent rope snapped in 1865?
questions.hint: Only Whymper and two guides, a father and son, came down alive.
questions.explain: Four died. The snapped rope is on show in Zermatt, and a rumour that it had been cut lingered.

questions.question: Whose ship was the Mary Rose, raised from the bed of the Solent in 1982?
questions.hint: It sank in 1545, leading an attack on a French fleet.
questions.explain: Henry VIII's. Its raising from the Solent in 1982 drew an estimated 60 million live TV viewers.

questions.question: In German, what is still called a 'Draisine', after Karl Drais's 1817 running machine?
questions.hint: It runs on rails.
questions.explain: A small railway inspection trolley. Riders pushed Drais's machine along with their feet; it had no pedals.

questions.question: After being raised in 2016, where was Amundsen's sunken polar ship Maud towed?
questions.hint: It crossed the Atlantic, heading home.
questions.explain: Maud ended up as a Hudson's Bay Company warehouse. It was raised in 2016 and reached Norway in 2018.

questions.question: Where did Bertha Benz buy fuel on her 1888 drive from Mannheim to Pforzheim?
questions.hint: Her fuel was a solvent also used as a stain remover.
questions.explain: Wiesloch's Stadt-Apotheke sold her about three litres of ligroin. Wiesloch calls it the world's first filling station.

questions.question: In 1899 La Jamais Contente became the first car to exceed 100 km/h. What powered it?
questions.hint: It carried neither a boiler nor a fuel tank.
questions.explain: Electricity. Camille Jenatzy's torpedo-shaped car hit 105.88 km/h near Paris; until 1902 the fastest cars were electric.

questions.question: How did Charles Lindbergh see straight ahead when flying the Spirit of St. Louis?
answers: Through a hole in the floor
questions.hint: The main fuel tank sat in front of the cockpit.
questions.explain: Through a periscope: the main fuel tank sat in front of the cockpit for safety, so there is no windscreen.

questions.question: Where did Amundsen's ship Gjøa, first through the Northwest Passage, spend the years 1909 to 1972?
questions.hint: Souvenir hunters damaged it there, far from Norway.
questions.explain: It was on show in San Francisco's Golden Gate Park until 1972; now it is at Oslo's Fram Museum.

questions.question: In 1919 Alcock and Brown's Vickers Vimy crossed the Atlantic non-stop. Where did it land?
answers: On the roof of Buckingham Palace
questions.hint: What looked like a meadow from the air was nothing of the sort.
questions.explain: It landed in a bog near Clifden, Galway: the 'meadow' was marsh, and the Vimy tipped onto its nose.

questions.question: What did the note in Amundsen's 1911 South Pole tent ask Scott to do?
answers: Forward a letter to Norway's king
Carry the tent back to Norway
questions.hint: Think of who in Norway Amundsen most wanted to hear the news.
questions.explain: It asked Scott to forward a letter to King Haakon. Scott found the tent a month later.

questions.question: The gold 'Last Spike' completed America's coast-to-coast railway in 1869. What happened to it next?
answers: It was sent to the Moon
questions.hint: It was only tapped into a hole drilled in advance.
questions.explain: It was tapped into a pre-drilled hole, then removed; ordinary spikes replaced it. Stanford University owns it now.

questions.question: What do the first-hand accounts of the Pilgrims' 1620 landing say about Plymouth Rock?
answers: They say it was solid gold
They say they prayed on it
questions.hint: Its fame as the landing place came long after 1620.
questions.explain: Neither first-hand account mentions a rock. It was identified as the landing place only around 1741.

questions.question: The Diamond Sutra of 868 is the world's oldest dated printed book. Where was it printed?
questions.hint: It is a Buddhist scroll, now in the British Library.
questions.explain: This Buddhist scroll was printed in China in 868, almost six centuries before Gutenberg's Bible.

questions.question: How did the Coronation Spoon survive when the Crown Jewels were destroyed in 1649?
answers: A dog buried it in a garden
questions.hint: It changed hands rather than being destroyed.
questions.explain: A royal wardrobe official bought it and returned it after the Restoration. It has been used at coronations ever since.

questions.question: In which modern country was the Code of Hammurabi, a Babylonian king's law stele, found?
questions.hint: An Elamite king had carried it off as war booty.
questions.explain: Iran. In the 12th century BC an Elamite king took it to Susa as booty; French excavators found it there.

questions.question: What creature appears on every piece of Wedgwood's table service for Catherine the Great?
questions.hint: Her palace for it came to be called after this creature.
questions.explain: A green frog, a nod to the palace the service was made for. Pieces also show hand-painted views of Britain.

questions.question: What does the Fitzwilliam Museum's Roman silver folding gadget combine?
questions.hint: The museum lists it as an eating implement.
questions.explain: A spoon, fork and knife. It also folds out a spike, a spatula and a pick.

questions.question: Why was Henry Cole's 1843 Christmas card, the first commercial one, controversial?
answers: It showed men gambling at cards
questions.hint: It came out when the temperance movement was growing.
questions.explain: It showed children drinking wine with the adults. Henry Cole had 1,000 printed and sold spares at a shilling each.

questions.question: Where did Hubert Booth's first vacuum cleaners, from 1901, stay while cleaning a building?
questions.hint: It was far too big, and drawn by horses.
questions.explain: Out in the street: horse-drawn engines worked from outside through long hoses.

questions.question: How did rubber, used for the India rubber eraser, get its English name?
questions.hint: Think of what the gum was used for in Britain.
questions.explain: From rubbing out: in Britain the South American gum was used to erase pencil marks.

questions.question: Around 1750, how did a woman in full British court dress get through a doorway?
questions.hint: Her skirts were very wide, but only in one direction.
questions.explain: Sideways. Side hoops of linen and whalebone held the skirts far out at the hips.

questions.question: Which British firm's self-locking brick came before Lego's first plastic bricks of 1949?
questions.hint: Its name is aimed at children.
questions.explain: Kiddicraft. Before its 1949 plastic bricks, Lego made wooden toys, ladders and ironing boards.

questions.question: Wham-O renamed its 'Pluto Platter' the Frisbee. Where does the name Frisbee come from?
questions.hint: Think of something students might toss once it was empty.
questions.explain: A pie company: the Frisbie baking company of Bridgeport, Connecticut. Wham-O borrowed the name and changed the spelling.

questions.question: Apollo 10's command module was called Charlie Brown. What was its lunar module called?
questions.hint: Think of Charlie Brown's dog in the Peanuts strip.
questions.explain: Snoopy flew to within about 14 km of the Moon; Charlie Brown is now in London's Science Museum.

questions.question: Which company polished the Hubble Space Telescope's backup mirror, the one without the flaw?
questions.hint: The company was based in Rochester, New York.
questions.explain: Kodak polished the spare, which never flew. It sat in storage for years, then went on display in Washington.

questions.question: Fans of which TV series got NASA's first Space Shuttle renamed Enterprise?
questions.hint: Leonard Nimoy, who played Spock, came to the roll-out.
questions.explain: Fans' letters got it renamed from Constitution; at its 1976 roll-out, a band played the Star Trek theme.

questions.question: What was found inside Liberty Bell 7, Gus Grissom's sunken capsule, once it was raised?
questions.hint: The find was made of metal.
questions.explain: Dozens of Mercury dimes, fitting for Project Mercury. The capsule had spent 38 years on the Atlantic floor.

questions.question: East London Museum's 1938 coelacanth proved coelacanths were not extinct. What happened to its insides?
answers: They are on show beside it
They were sold to a collector
questions.hint: The insides were neither kept nor sold.
questions.explain: Its insides were thrown away before a scientist could study them. Science had known coelacanths only as fossils.

questions.question: Oxford's Megalosaurus jaw belongs to the first dinosaur ever named. What does 'Megalosaurus' mean?
questions.hint: It describes the animal's size, not its temper.
questions.explain: Megalosaurus means 'great lizard'. It was named in 1824, before the word 'dinosaur' existed.

questions.question: Who advised sculptor Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins on the Crystal Palace dinosaurs?
questions.hint: He had named the Dinosauria in 1842.
questions.explain: Richard Owen, who had named the Dinosauria in 1842, advised Hawkins; in 1853 Hawkins held a dinner inside the mould of his Iguanodon.

questions.question: London's Natural History Museum keeps the platypus type specimen. Why isn't the animal's scientific name Platypus?
answers: A beetle genus already had it
questions.hint: The trouble was the name itself, not the specimen or its publication.
questions.explain: 'Platypus' already belonged to a genus of ambrosia beetles, so Blumenbach's Ornithorhynchus replaced it.

questions.question: Teylers Museum's 'Haarlem Archaeopteryx' was called a pterosaur, then an Archaeopteryx. What is it now?
questions.hint: It is a genuine fossil, and not a pterosaur.
questions.explain: Now Ostromia, a dinosaur genus named after John Ostrom, who unmasked the 'pterosaur' in 1970.

questions.question: What brought down Father Time, the weathervane at Lord's, during the Second World War?
questions.hint: It came from London's own air defences, not the enemy.
questions.explain: A barrage balloon's cable tore it down, not a bomb. Lightning also struck it, in 1992.

questions.question: Which country won the America's Cup from the New York Yacht Club in 1983?
questions.hint: The winning boat sailed for a nation in the southern hemisphere.
questions.explain: Australia's 1983 win ended the New York Yacht Club's 132-year hold. Garrard made the trophy in 1848.

questions.question: Since 1928, golf's Open champions have lifted a replica Claret Jug. Where does the original stay?
questions.hint: The original stays with the R&A, at its clubhouse in Scotland.
questions.explain: The original, first presented in 1873, stays in St Andrews. Walter Hagen was the first champion handed the replica.

questions.question: Where did the ball from the 1966 World Cup final spend the next 30 years?
questions.hint: It spent those years outside England.
questions.explain: West Germany's Helmut Haller took it home. In 1996 the Mirror, Virgin and Eurostar paid £80,000 for it.

questions.question: How did the thief get into the Ashmolean to take its Cézanne?
questions.hint: Think of the fireworks over Oxford.
questions.explain: Through the roof: a thief came in from above while millennium fireworks covered the noise.

questions.question: Jenner protected a boy from smallpox with material from a milkmaid’s hand. Which disease did she have?
questions.hint: A mild relative of the disease Jenner fought.
questions.explain: Cowpox: Jenner took material from the milkmaid's hand to protect a boy from smallpox.

questions.question: The song widely considered the oldest complete composition is carved on a stone. Which country's national museum holds it?
questions.hint: Not the country where it was found.
questions.explain: The Seikilos stele, found in Turkey, is in the National Museum of Denmark in Copenhagen.

questions.question: The vivid blue in Hokusai's Great Wave came partly from a new pigment. Where was it imported from?
questions.hint: It is named after a German kingdom.
questions.explain: Europe: Prussian blue, also called Berlin blue, was imported for printing in Japan.

questions.question: The Lewis Chessmen, found on a Scottish island, were carved from sperm whale teeth and which other material?
questions.hint: It comes from a tusk, though not an elephant's.
questions.explain: Walrus ivory: the pieces are made of walrus ivory and sperm whale teeth.

questions.question: The famous 'Timur Ruby' in the Royal Collection is not a ruby. What is it?
questions.hint: It is a genuine gemstone, just not the one in its name.
questions.explain: It is a red spinel, a different mineral from ruby. It sits in a necklace made for Queen Victoria in 1853.

questions.question: William Herschel first named the planet we call Uranus after whom?
questions.hint: He was hoping the name would win him a royal patron.
questions.explain: He called it Georgium Sidus, 'George's Star', after King George III, who then hired him as his astronomer.

questions.question: What sits on top of the Wimbledon men's singles trophy?
questions.hint: It is something you could eat.
questions.explain: A pineapple tops the trophy, first presented in 1887. Even the club says it does not know why.

questions.question: In 2014 the Smithsonian took in a cartridge dug out of a New Mexico landfill. Which Atari game was it?
questions.hint: Think of a film alien who wanted to phone home.
questions.explain: Atari dumped unsold stock near Alamogordo in 1983. The 2014 dig found hundreds of E.T. cartridges, and one went to the Smithsonian.

questions.question: Before he flew the Channel in 1909, what had Louis Blériot made his money from?
questions.hint: It was an accessory for the new motor car.
questions.explain: Blériot was a successful maker of car headlamps before he crossed the Channel in his Type XI in 1909.

questions.question: How did the body of Martha, the last passenger pigeon, travel to the Smithsonian in 1914?
answers: Frozen in a block of ice
Pickled in a jar of brandy
Packed in a crate of salt
questions.hint: Think of how a fishmonger kept things fresh before the refrigerator.
questions.explain: Martha died at Cincinnati Zoo in 1914 and went to Washington by train, frozen in a block of ice.

questions.question: In the 1700s, what was blown into apparently drowned people to try to revive them?
questions.hint: It came from a plant, burned in a small box.
questions.explain: A tobacco resuscitator: its bellows pumped in air, or tobacco smoke through the rectum, to revive the apparently drowned. A London society founded in 1774 promoted it.

questions.question: On Gemini 3 in 1965, what floated around the cabin after one bite of a smuggled sandwich?
questions.hint: The bread did not hold together.
questions.explain: Crumbs of rye bread. John Young smuggled the corned beef sandwich aboard in 1965, and a House committee later looked into it.

questions.question: In 2005 thieves took a two-tonne Henry Moore bronze from his old estate. What do police believe became of it?
questions.hint: Think less about art dealers and more about what two tonnes of bronze is worth to a metal yard.
questions.explain: Police came to believe it was melted down for scrap, worth a tiny fraction of its value as a sculpture.

questions.question: Julia Child’s kitchen, now in the Smithsonian, has counters built higher than standard for her. By how much?
questions.hint: Enough to spare a tall cook’s back, not enough to need a step stool.
questions.explain: Her counters were made two inches higher than standard because she was very tall.

questions.question: The first crossword ran in a New York paper in 1913. What did its creator, Arthur Wynne, call it?
questions.hint: The same two words as today, just the other way round.
questions.explain: Wynne called it a ‘word-cross’. The name flipped to ‘cross-word’ later, apparently through a typesetter’s error.

questions.question: Why did steam from hot tea trouble the Victorian owners of moustache cups?
answers: It set off the fire alarm
questions.hint: Gentlemen used something stiff to keep the ends of a moustache in shape.
questions.explain: Steam melted moustache wax; the cup's ledge kept the moustache, and the wax, out of the drink.

questions.question: A 1958 fire at New York's Museum of Modern Art cost it a large Monet. What finally wrecked the painting?
questions.hint: It happened while people were trying to help.
questions.explain: MoMA's own account says firefighters, breaking in through the windows, unknowingly destroyed the large Water Lilies.

questions.question: Newark's Civil War coins are stamped OBS. What does it stand for?
questions.hint: The town was surrounded by enemy armies when the coins were made.
questions.explain: Under siege. OBS is Latin shorthand for the siege, stamped on coins cut from silver plate.

questions.question: What did William Renshaw do with the Field Cup, Wimbledon's first singles trophy?
answers: Kept it, as the rules allowed
Used it as a tennis ball
questions.hint: Today's champions get a replica, partly because of what he did.
questions.explain: He kept it: under the rules a three-time winner could, and he later kept the next cup too. The Field Cup is now on show in the Wimbledon museum.

questions.question: Which people made the Dresden Codex, a book of astronomical tables?
questions.hint: It is written in hieroglyphs and dates from before Europeans reached the Americas.
questions.explain: The Maya. It is one of the few Maya books to survive, and is kept in Dresden.

questions.question: Boston's mint struck pine tree shillings until 1682. What date do nearly all of them carry?
questions.hint: The coins kept the year the mint was founded, not the year they were made.
questions.explain: 1652, the year the Massachusetts mint was founded. The date stayed the same until the mint closed in 1682.

questions.question: Goya's Duke of Wellington, stolen from the National Gallery in 1961, was found in 1965. Where?
answers: Inside the clock of Big Ben
questions.hint: Travellers leave their bags in this sort of place.
questions.explain: A left-luggage office in Birmingham. In between, the stolen portrait had a guest appearance in the 1962 Bond film Dr. No.

questions.question: What did Florence Nightingale actually carry on her night rounds at Scutari?
questions.hint: Think local: it came from the country she was working in, not from her portraits.
questions.explain: A Turkish lantern, a fanoos, not the genie lamp of her portraits.

questions.question: Until 1994, what did botanists believe about the Wollemi pine?
answers: It was a kind of seaweed
questions.hint: Its relatives were known mainly from very old rocks.
questions.explain: It was thought long extinct, until a park officer found living trees in a canyon in 1994.

questions.question: On the Apollo 11 customs form of 1969, what was declared as cargo?
answers: Moon rock and Moon dust samples
questions.hint: Think of what the crew actually brought home from the surface.
questions.explain: Moon rock and Moon dust samples. The form also gave the departure point as the Moon, though it was probably a joke rather than official paperwork.

questions.question: How many times has Rembrandt's portrait of Jacob de Gheyn III been stolen from Dulwich Picture Gallery?
questions.hint: Its nickname is 'the takeaway Rembrandt', so more than once, but not absurdly often.
questions.explain: Four times. The small portrait is known as the takeaway Rembrandt; once a thief rode off with it on a bicycle.

questions.question: Snakes and ladders grew out of an old Indian board game. What was that game for?
questions.hint: Every snake and every ladder once stood for a way of behaving.
questions.explain: It taught morality: virtues sent you up a ladder, vices down a snake, towards a higher or lower realm.

questions.question: The oldest known bread, found at Shubayqa 1 in Jordan, is about 14,400 years old. Who baked it?
questions.hint: It is older than the first fields of cultivated grain.
questions.explain: Natufian hunter-gatherers baked it from wild cereals, at least 4,000 years before agriculture began.

questions.question: Röntgen's famous 1895 X-ray of his wife's hand shows her bones and one other thing. What?
questions.hint: X-rays passed through her flesh but not through bone or metal.
questions.explain: Her wedding ring: the rays left bones and metal visible, so the gold ring stands out around her finger.

questions.question: Tin cans of food came first. How long did people wait for a can opener?
questions.hint: Early cans were thick iron, and a hammer did the job for a long while.
questions.explain: About fifty years: until thinner cans and patented openers arrived, people used a hammer and chisel.

questions.question: In the First World War, where did the British Museum keep the Rosetta Stone safe?
questions.hint: Its keepers wanted it below ground, safe from bombs.
questions.explain: A Post Office railway station: the Stone waited out the air raids on a platform of the mail railway being built under London.

questions.question: Marco Polo saw Kublai Khan's paper money being made. What was the paper made from?
questions.hint: It came from the same tree whose leaves fed the silkworms.
questions.explain: Mulberry bark: Polo describes the fine layer under the mulberry tree's outer bark made into sheets of paper money.

cases.title: The Stolen World Cup
cases.role: You are a young detective constable at Scotland Yard in March 1966, newly assigned to the hunt for the stolen World Cup.

steps.text: Sunday 20 March 1966. You are sent to Central Hall, Westminster, where a stamp exhibition has borrowed the World Cup from the Football Association. England hosts the tournament in July. Guards checked the glass case at 11 a.m. By about 12.10 it was empty.

steps.label: Exhibit A
steps.title: Stamps left behind
steps.text: Stamps valued at about £3 million lie untouched. The trophy was insured for £30,000, though its official value was only £3,000.

steps.label: Exhibit B
steps.title: A call, then a parcel
steps.text: FA chairman Joe Mears receives a piece from the top of the trophy and a note demanding £15,000. Tell the police, it warns, and the cup will be melted down.

steps.question: Mears ignores the warning and tells Scotland Yard. A caller, 'Jackson', wants cash. What goes in the suitcase?

options.text: The full £15,000 in cash
options.reply: The police advised against paying the ransom; the bundles were mostly paper.

options.text: Paper bundles with real notes outside
options.reply: Bundles of paper with real banknotes on the outside made the suitcase look full of money, as the police intended.

options.text: Nothing: an empty case
options.reply: Jackson was shown the suitcase before they drove off, so it had to look convincing.

steps.text: Friday 25 March. Mears is in bed with angina, so a Flying Squad detective speaks for him, posing as his assistant, 'Mr McPhee'. The detective drives Mears's car to Battersea Park, where Jackson gets in. You follow in an unmarked car.

steps.question: On the drive, Jackson grows nervous, then jumps from the car and runs. What has he spotted?

options.text: Paper inside the bundles
options.reply: He had been shown the money before they set off; it was the police tail, not the cash, that made him bolt.

options.text: That Mears is not there
options.reply: He already knew. After some hesitation on the phone, he had agreed to deal with Mears's 'assistant', Mr McPhee.

options.text: A van that keeps following them
options.reply: He recognised a van trailing the car as a Flying Squad type, which it was. He was caught minutes later in Kennington.

steps.text: The man says he was only a go-between for someone he calls 'The Pole'. The trophy is still missing. Sunday 27 March, about 9 p.m., Upper Norwood: David Corbett, a Thames lighterman, steps out to make a phone call with his dog, Pickles.

steps.label: Exhibit C
steps.title: A parcel by a parked car
steps.text: Propped against a car wheel by the hedge: newspaper, tightly tied with string. Torn open, it shows a gilded woman raising a cup, and winners' names on the base.

steps.question: Corbett takes the parcel to the police. What happens to him next?

options.text: He is questioned as a suspect
options.reply: He was questioned as a possible suspect, then cleared of any part in the theft.

options.text: He is paid a reward at once
options.reply: Rewards came only later, and added up to several thousand pounds.

options.text: He is thanked and sent home
options.reply: Not at first. He and the trophy were taken to Cannon Row police station, where it was identified as genuine.

steps.text: A week after the theft, the trophy was back. Corbett was cleared, and Pickles became a celebrity, joining the players' celebration dinner after England's 4–2 World Cup final win over West Germany on 30 July. The go-between was jailed for two years for demanding money with menaces. Who actually took the trophy has never been established.

cases.now: Brazil won the trophy outright in 1970; stolen in Rio in 1983, it was never found. FIFA bought the FA's 1966 replica in 1997; it is kept at Manchester's National Football Museum.

cases.title: Three Seconds in Barcelona
cases.role: You are a junior calculator in Paris in 1805, hired to copy the late Pierre Méchain's survey notebooks.

steps.text: Paris, 22 June 1799. A bar of platinum is presented to the legislature and then locked in the national archives. It is the new metre: one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator, fixed by seven years of surveying from Dunkirk to Barcelona.

steps.question: The arc from Dunkirk to Barcelona is just over 1,000 km long. How did two astronomers measure it?

options.text: A chain of triangles, checked by stars
options.reply: They measured the angles of a long chain of triangles with Borda's new repeating circle, and fixed the latitudes along the line by observing stars.

options.text: Measuring rods laid end to end
options.reply: No. Rods were used only on short measured baselines; every other distance in the chain was worked out from the angles.

options.text: Counting the paces of a walker
options.reply: Far too crude. Borda's new repeating circle measured angles more accurately than the older quadrant, a precision no pacing could match.

steps.text: Méchain took the southern end. In the winter of 1792–93 he fixed the latitude at the fortress of Montjuïc above Barcelona. In 1793 an accident at a water pump nearly killed him, and war between France and Spain kept him in the city.

steps.label: Exhibit A
steps.title: Méchain's Barcelona register
steps.text: The fortress is now closed to him. From December 1793 he observes the stars from the terrace of his inn, the Fontana de Oro, through the winter.

steps.label: Exhibit B
steps.title: Two stations, two answers
steps.text: Triangles link the inn and the fortress, about 2 km apart. Carried across, the two latitudes should agree. They differ by about 3 seconds of arc, roughly 100 metres.

steps.question: Méchain cannot return to Montjuïc to check. What does he do about the gap?

options.text: Keeps it secret
options.reply: He told no one, not the international commission, not Delambre, not his assistant, and for years pressed to go back to Spain.

options.text: Reports it to Paris straight away
options.reply: No. His Montjuïc results had already gone to Paris as the anchor of the whole chain, and he never disclosed the gap.

options.text: Averages the two latitudes
options.reply: No. The Montjuïc figures were already in Paris, and the metre was computed from them; the inn's figures were never used.

steps.text: The metre was fixed on the Montjuïc figures. In 1803 Méchain returned to Spain to extend the survey south to the Balearic Islands. He died of fever at Castellón de la Plana on 20 September 1804. His papers passed to Delambre.

steps.question: Delambre, writing the official account, now sees the gap. What does he print?

options.text: Both sets of figures, side by side
options.reply: In volume 2 of the Base du système métrique, 1807, he printed the inn's observations beside Montjuïc's and did not hide the gap.

options.text: Only the Montjuïc figures
options.reply: No. He recalculated all the Barcelona data and printed it, after checking it against Méchain's original notes.

options.text: The full story of the cover-up
options.reply: No. He kept Méchain's concealment out of print, sealed his letters in the Observatory archives and left a frank account published only in 1912.

steps.question: So how far out is the platinum metre, and why?

options.text: About 0.2 mm, mostly the Earth's shape
options.reply: It is about 0.2 mm shorter than a ten-millionth of the quarter meridian, mainly because the Earth is less regular than the shape assumed in 1799.

options.text: Several centimetres, because of Méchain
options.reply: Far less. Carried into the whole arc, even the full gap would have been about 0.01 per cent, and the inn's figures were never used.

options.text: Not at all; it is exact
options.reply: No. It is about 0.2 mm short, and the provisional metre of 1793, based on an older survey, was actually closer to the target.

steps.text: Méchain had made no real blunder, though he had hidden the gap and altered some readings to make them look more consistent. Later astronomers reworked his figures and reconciled them: small effects, such as refraction and instrument error, added up to the gap. The metre stayed as it was, about 0.2 mm short of its target, and every later definition has kept that length.

cases.now: The platinum Mètre des Archives is kept by the Archives nationales in Paris, in the iron cabinet, the armoire de fer, at the Hôtel de Soubise, beside France's constitutions.

catalog.title: Schabowski's note
catalog.note: Thought lost for over 20 years. Bought by Germany's House of History in 2015 for €25,000.

story: On the evening of 9 November 1989, Politburo member Günter Schabowski gave a press conference in East Berlin, broadcast live on East German television. Just before seven, he read out new travel rules from a typed draft: private trips abroad could be applied for without preconditions.

A journalist asked when the rules would take effect. Schabowski searched his papers and answered: “As far as I know… immediately, without delay.” He did not know the rules were meant to start the next morning.
The news spread on television in East and West. Thousands went to the border crossings. Around 11:30 p.m., the crossing at Bornholmer Strasse opened first.

His handwritten notes from that evening, with the line "read out travel regulation text", were thought lost for more than twenty years. They resurfaced in 2015, when Germany's House of History foundation bought them for 25,000 euros.

exhibits.claim: The theft that made her world-famous.

catalog.title: The Mona Lisa
catalog.note: Missing 28 months. Recovered in Florence in December 1913.

story: On Monday 21 August 1911, when the Louvre was closed, Vincenzo Peruggia, a glazier who had once fitted protective glass there, lifted a small painting on a poplar panel off its four iron hooks, hid it under his white workman's smock and walked out.
For a day, nobody raised the alarm. When the museum reopened, crowds queued to stare at the empty wall. The police even questioned Pablo Picasso, who was cleared.
More than two years later, in Florence, the thief offered the painting to the art dealer Alfredo Geri. He was arrested at his hotel in December 1913.
Before the theft, she was a masterpiece. After it, she was world-famous.

story: Before dawn on 12 February 1994, the day the Lillehammer Winter Olympics opened, two men leaned a ladder against Norway's National Gallery in Oslo. One climbed up, smashed a window, cut the wire Edvard Munch's The Scream hung on and brought it out the same way. It took about fifty seconds.
They left a postcard thanking the museum for the poor security. The guard had taken the alarm for a false one.
Almost three months later, a British detective posed as a buyer for California's Getty Museum. On 7 May 1994 the police recovered the painting in Åsgårdstrand, a small seaside town.
Munch painted more than one Scream. In 2004, gunmen took another version from the Munch Museum; it was recovered in 2006.

story: At 1:24 a.m. on 18 March 1990, the night after St Patrick's Day, two men in police uniforms rang at the side door of the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. The night guard let them in. Minutes later both guards were handcuffed in the basement.

The thieves stayed eighty-one minutes. They cut Rembrandt's only seascape from its frame and took thirteen works in all, among them a Vermeer, a Manet, drawings by Degas and the bronze eagle from a Napoleonic flag.
Decades later, no one has been charged and nothing has been recovered. The museum promised up to ten million dollars for information leading to the works' return.
The museum keeps five of the empty frames as placeholders for the missing works.
